faq.q: What's the difference between the three removal modes?
faq.a: 'Strip everything' re-encodes the image through a canvas, which also re-compresses the pixels. 'Strip all, but keep orientation' and 'Strip GPS only (keep camera data)' rewrite the original JPEG bytes directly with no re-compression, so the pixels are untouched. Use GPS-only when you want to hide your location but keep camera, date and exposure data.

faq.q: Does 'Strip GPS only' actually erase the coordinates or just hide them?
faq.a: It erases them. The tool overwrites every byte the GPS IFD owns — including the latitude/longitude rational values stored elsewhere — with zeros in place, then removes the GPS pointer. This matters because an earlier approach that only zeroed the pointer left the real coordinates readable by a hex editor or forensic tool.

faq.q: Can it read GPS and camera data from PNG and WebP, or only JPEG?
faq.a: It reads full EXIF — camera make/model, lens, date, ISO, aperture, and GPS — from JPEG, PNG (eXIf chunk) and WebP (EXIF chunk). It also handles photos where XMP comes before EXIF. However, the byte-level GPS-only and keep-orientation strips apply to JPEG; PNG/WebP go through the canvas re-encode path.

faq.q: Why did my portrait photo come back rotated after stripping everything?
faq.a: It shouldn't anymore. A phone stores pixels in sensor orientation plus an Orientation tag; stripping all tags removes that tag. For JPEGs with a rotation tag, the tool draws the already-rotated decoded image onto a canvas, baking the correct orientation into the pixels so no tag is needed. GPS warnings also appear with an OpenStreetMap link before removal.
